summary: Collects best current practices for running Network Time Protocol servers and clients on the Internet. It gives recommendations aimed at making time service stable, accurate, and secure, and targets NTP version 4 as described in RFC 5905. It is a guidance document rather than a new protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Clocks on computers need to agree, like classmates checking the same wall clock. This is a checklist of good habits for the people who run the computers that share the time.

questions: how many ntp servers should i use
subtitle: A checklist of habits for running NTP servers and clients accurately, stably and securely.

tldr.problem: NTP is widely used, but sloppy configuration and unprotected packets make time service inaccurate and open to abuse such as amplification attacks and spoofing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects recommendations for NTPv4 operators and implementers: use at least four diverse sources, limit control messages, handle leap seconds carefully, protect packets, monitor for attack signatures and respect Kiss-o'-Death packets.
tldr.outcome: It is guidance, not a new protocol. Following it makes time distribution more reliable and harder to attack.

today: RFC 8633 is a Best Current Practice published in July 2019. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It targets NTPv4 as defined in RFC 5905.

sections.title: Scope and Audience
sections.content:
NTP version 4 has been widely used since its publication as RFC 5905. RFC 8633 is a collection of best practices for operating NTP clients and servers, aimed at helping operators distribute time more accurately and securely. It is meant to apply to a broad range of networks. Some networks have stricter accuracy needs and will need extra techniques.

It covers general network security, protocol-specific security, server and client configuration, and NTP in embedded devices. It also holds information for implementers who want to build their own implementation compliant with RFC 5905. Appendix A lists practices specific to the Network Time Foundation implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a how-to-be-careful guide for people who keep computer clocks right.

sections.title: Time Sources and Reference Clocks
sections.content:
An RFC 5905 implementation feeds its time sources into intersection, clustering and combining algorithms to estimate the correct time. How many sources you have matters. With one source, any error is passed on. With two, a disagreement cannot be resolved without outside information. With three, losing one source is tolerable but you fall back to the two-source case. With four or more diverse sources, losing one still leaves three.

Operators who care about accurate time SHOULD use at least four independent, diverse sources. Fewer is allowed (MAY) but carries the risks above. The analysis assumes most servers are honest. If an attacker controls the network, all servers' time could be compromised.

Diversity applies to hardware reference clocks as well. Devices from one vendor may share bugs, and even different vendors may share a chipset or firmware. Satellite navigation services can have systemic faults, and sunspot activity can make satellite or radio time sources unusable, so operators may need a backup plan.

Even four sources can disagree. Around the June 2015 leap second, some operators used leap smearing and others did not, so two of many clients' four sources gave UTC/POSIX time and two gave smeared time. Operators should monitor all sources and investigate or drop ones that do not align.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask only one friend what time it is and they are wrong, you are wrong too. Ask four different friends and you can spot the one who is off.

sections.title: Control Messages, Monitoring and Pools
sections.content:
Some NTPv4 implementations provide control messages (Mode 6), first specified in an appendix of RFC 1305 and not part of RFC 5905. They allow monitoring and optionally authenticated control, but can be abused for amplification attacks because responses are much larger than queries. Public-facing servers are RECOMMENDED to block control queries from outside their organization, and use beyond basic monitoring SHOULD need an authenticated session with a controlkey or an access control list.

Many attacks rely on forged source addresses, and UDP-based protocols such as NTP are more susceptible than connection-oriented ones. The RFC recommends that ISPs and large corporate networks implement ingress and egress filtering as described in BCP 38 (RFC 2827).

Operators SHOULD use remote monitoring and read system logs. Replies that match no request can mean someone is forging the system's address to make a server throttle it. Early messages seen by a broadcast client can mean forged broadcast packets, and timestamps much earlier than the system time can mean a fast clock or a replay attack.

Operators MUST only synchronize to servers they have permission to use. The NTP Pool Project is a volunteer service whose time is generally good but carries no guarantee, and vendors can obtain their own pool subdomain. Large networks may run local servers synchronized to the pool.
sections.plainLanguage: Some settings let strangers ask your clock very big questions, which can be used to flood someone else. Keep those doors locked, watch the logs, and only borrow time from servers that said yes.

sections.title: Leap Seconds and Leap Smearing
sections.content:
UTC is kept within 0.9 seconds of UT1 by inserting, or possibly deleting, a leap second. Every leap second since 1972 has been positive, and NTP also supports a negative one. NTP time is based on UTC, and servers can pass on leap-second notices. RFC 5905 says leap seconds are applied only on the last day of a month, so servers are RECOMMENDED to wait until that day before announcing one, because some older clients apply it at the end of the current day. Clients should not use polling intervals above 24 hours so the notice is not missed.

Leap smearing spreads the adjustment over a smear interval instead of adding or removing a second. Periods from two to twenty-four hours have been used successfully. During the window clients may be off UTC by up to a full second but agree with each other. It helps systems that mishandle a 61-second (or 59-second) minute.

The rules are firm. Operators with legal or strong requirements to match UTC SHOULD NOT smear. Clients of smearing servers MUST NOT apply standard leap handling or load a leap-second file. Smearing MUST NOT be used on public-facing servers, since there is no standard way for a client to detect it, and a client MUST NOT mix smeared and non-smeared servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the world adds one extra second to the day. Smearing is like stretching every second a tiny bit all day instead of adding one big second at the end, but everyone has to agree to stretch.

sections.title: Protecting NTP Packets
sections.content:
By default NTP packets are unprotected, so a man in the middle can drop, replay or modify them. NTP has two internal mechanisms that add a Message Authentication Code (MAC) to protect authenticity and integrity. Neither encrypts the payload, since it is not considered confidential. RFC 7384 analyzes threats to time protocols.

The pre-shared key approach uses a symmetric key per association. NTP has no key exchange, so keys MUST be exchanged securely by other means and protected. Each association is RECOMMENDED to have its own key, and keys should be refreshed periodically. RFC 5905 specifies MD5, which is now considered too weak (see RFC 6151). Users SHOULD use AES-128-CMAC (RFC 8573) once available. Keys stored in clear text MUST be readable only by the NTP process.

Autokey (RFC 5906) was published in 2010, but researchers found vulnerabilities and it SHOULD NOT be used. Work on a replacement, Network Time Security, was in progress at the time of writing. External protocols such as IPsec and MACsec can add protection but may reduce synchronization performance. None of these measures prevents packet delay manipulation attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: A secret handshake between two computers proves a message really came from the right one. Some old handshakes are too easy to fake, so use a newer one.

sections.title: Security Practices for Servers and Clients
sections.content:
Limit leaked information. The base NTP packet reveals fields such as the reference ID and reference time, and control queries reveal more. Access control lists SHOULD limit who can see this, and hosts SHOULD only answer control queries from authorized parties. A leaf-node host, which only sets its own clock, SHOULD drop all incoming NTP packets except mode 4 responses from known sources.

Daemon restart attacks. RFC 5905 says a client should not accept an offset above the panic threshold of 1000 s. If the operating system restarts the daemon automatically and the client ignores the panic threshold on restarts, an attacker can send a huge offset, cause the exit, and have it accepted after restart. Operators SHOULD NOT ignore the panic threshold in all cold starts without strong oversight. Mitigations include monitoring logs, requiring manual intervention, and raising the number of servers required before adjusting the clock.

Attack signatures. Operators SHOULD watch for bogus packets (origin timestamp not matching), zero origin packets, and packets with an invalid MAC.

Kiss-o'-Death. Devices are RECOMMENDED to honor KoD RATE packets and back off, but a client MUST accept one only with a valid origin timestamp, and should not raise its poll interval value past 13 (two hours). Because KoD packets are often accepted unauthenticated, they can be used for denial of service.

Modes. Broadcast mode shares one key among all clients, so any client could forge server messages; it SHOULD only run inside a trusted network. A host SHOULD only allow symmetric passive associations with trusted, authenticated peers, each under a different key.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not shout your secrets, do not let one bad message make your clock jump a whole lot, and only trust friends who know the secret word.

sections.title: Embedded Devices and Anycast
sections.content:
Embedded devices often lack a battery-backed clock, so NTP may be needed at power-up, and they face the same threats as other hosts. Customers usually cannot update the NTP implementation themselves, so vendors are responsible for keeping it current and SHOULD allow the device's server list to be updated. Vendors MUST only preconfigure servers they have permission to use, and are encouraged to run their own time service, for example through the NTP Pool Project. RFC 4085 advises against embedding globally routable IP addresses.

Anycast (BCP 126, RFC 4786) gives one IP address to many servers so routers direct packets to the closest active one. It simplifies configuring many clients, but a single anycast address means each client likely has only one time source and loses the benefit of comparing several. Using multiple separate anycast pools helps. Switching servers can also shift a client's time slightly, so operators are RECOMMENDED to deploy anycast NTP only where applications tolerate that.

Servers are RECOMMENDED to monitor NTP performance independently and withdraw from the anycast network when they misbehave, and to have an alternate unicast address. A suggested hybrid has Stratum 1 servers on unicast interfaces, with Stratum 2 servers at each site offering both a unicast and a per-site anycast address.
sections.plainLanguage: Smart gadgets cannot fix themselves later, so their makers must pick good time servers up front. Sharing one phone number across many helpers is handy, but you should still check with more than one helper.
